questions.q: Why is dry acetone the solvent of choice when ethyl bromide is converted into ethyl iodide with NaI?
options: Acetone reacts with NaI to give free I₂, the actual reagent
Acetone is protic and solvates the bromide ion strongly
Acetone stabilises the ethyl carbocation formed in the reaction
NaI dissolves in acetone but NaBr does not, so NaBr precipitates and drives the equilibrium forward
questions.explain: The halogen exchange is an equilibrium; removal of NaBr (or NaCl) as a precipitate pulls it towards the alkyl iodide by Le Chatelier's principle. The reaction is SN2, so no carbocation is involved.

questions.q: (R)-2-Bromobutane is warmed with NaI in dry acetone. The organic product is:
questions.explain: The Finkelstein reaction is SN2, so iodide attacks from the back and the configuration is inverted (Walden inversion). Racemisation would require an SN1 path, which does not operate here.

questions.q: Which halide does NOT give an alkyl iodide when heated with NaI in dry acetone?
questions.explain: Fluoride is a very poor leaving group and the C–F bond is very strong, so iodide cannot displace it. Only chlorides, bromides and sulfonates are converted; including F among the replaceable halogens is a common mistake.

questions.q: In the sodium iodide in acetone test, which halide would be slowest to give a precipitate (or give none at all)?
questions.explain: The test relies on SN2 halogen exchange, so a tertiary halide is practically unreactive because of steric hindrance. Allyl, benzyl and primary halides react fast and quickly precipitate NaCl or NaBr.
